title: Fundamental Elliptic Curve Cryptography Algorithms
summary: Describes the fundamental algorithms of elliptic curve cryptography as defined in seminal work from 1994 and earlier. It covers only curves over fields of characteristic greater than three, and is useful for implementing the basic algorithms without later specialized optimizations. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Elliptic curves are a kind of math puzzle used to keep secrets. This note explains the original, basic way to solve the puzzle with a computer.

subtitle: The original, unoptimized recipes for elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman and ElGamal-style signatures, written down in one citable place.

tldr.problem: Elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) was adopted more slowly than expected, perhaps because of a lack of freely available normative documents and uncertainty over intellectual property rights.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC restates the fundamental ECC algorithms from seminal references dated 1994 and earlier: the group operation on curves over fields of characteristic greater than three, Diffie-Hellman key exchange (ECDH), and two ElGamal-style signature methods (KT-IV and KT-I).
tldr.outcome: It is detailed enough to serve as a normative reference, and it interoperates with parts of IKE, ANSI X9.62 and IEEE P1363 when parameters and options are chosen suitably. It is Informational.

today: RFC 6090 is an Informational RFC published in February 2011, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains a plain-language reference for the fundamental ECC algorithms.

sections.title: Why a Plain Description of ECC
sections.content:
ECC is a public-key technology that offers performance advantages at higher security levels. It includes an elliptic curve version of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange and elliptic curve versions of the ElGamal signature algorithm. The RFC says adoption was slower than anticipated, perhaps because of the lack of freely available normative documents and uncertainty over intellectual property rights.

The note therefore describes the fundamental algorithms, based directly on the original references and following their notation as closely as possible. Only curves over fields of characteristic greater than three are in scope; these are the curves used in Suite B. Sections 2 through 6 are normative; the rest is informative.
sections.eli5: People were slow to use this kind of math partly because nobody had written the plain recipe down in a free, official place. This document is that recipe.

sections.title: Elliptic Curve Groups and Parameters
sections.content:
After a review of modular arithmetic, groups and the finite field Fp, the RFC defines the curve by the equation y^2 = x^3 + a*x + b, with x, y, a and b in Fp and a nonzero discriminant. A point is a pair (x,y) that satisfies the equation, or the special point at infinity, which is the identity element. The inverse of (x1,y1) is (x1,-y1).

The group operation combines two points into a third using explicit formulas for the cases where the points differ and where they are equal. Pairs of integers that do not satisfy the equation are not valid points. Homogeneous coordinates (X,Y,Z) offer an alternative that is typically more efficient because it avoids a modular inversion.

A parameter set consists of the prime p, the values a and b, the generator g and the order n of the subgroup it generates. The order of that subgroup MUST be divisible by a large prime. Parameter sets with b = 0 and p = 3 (mod 4), or a = 0 and p = 2 (mod 3), are inferior and SHOULD NOT be used. Parameter generation is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Imagine a special kind of curvy graph where you can add two dots to get a third dot. The rules for adding are fixed, so everyone gets the same answer.

sections.title: Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman lets two parties on an insecure channel agree on a secret key. Party A picks a random exponent j between 1 and t-1, computes g^j and sends it to B. Party B picks k, computes g^k and sends it to A. Each side can then compute g^(j*k).

The RFC also describes compact output, where only the x-coordinate of the shared point is used as the secret, and compact representation, where only the x-coordinate of a public point is transmitted. Both parties in a run MUST use the same method, and if compact representation is used then compact output MUST be used as well.
sections.eli5: Two friends each mix a secret color into a shared paint, swap the mixes, and add their own secret again. They both end up with the same final color, and nobody watching can work it out.

sections.title: KT-IV and KT-I Signatures
sections.content:
Two ElGamal-style signature methods are described. Both need a collision-resistant hash function, so that messages of any length can be signed and existential forgery is avoided. Keypairs are the same in both: the private key z is a random integer between 1 and q-1, and the public key is Y = alpha^z.

KT-IV comes from Koyama and Tsuruoka. A signature is a pair (s1, s2) where s1 is the x-coordinate of alpha^k reduced modulo q for a fresh random k, and s2 = k/(h(m) + z*s1) mod q. KT-I computes the second component as s2 = (h(m) + z*s1)/k mod q, the same way as the Digital Signature Algorithm. A KT-IV signature (s1, s2) converts into the KT-I signature (s1, 1/s2 mod q) using only public information.

Verifiers MUST reject a signature unless 0 < s1 < q and 0 < s2 < q. The Rationale section notes that a valid signature with s2 = 0 would leak the secret key.
sections.eli5: A signature is like a stamp only you can make but anyone can check. KT-IV and KT-I are two slightly different stamp recipes, and you can turn one stamp into the other without knowing the secret.

sections.title: Interoperability and Testing
sections.content:
The ECDH of this note can be used with IKE versions one and two, and is compatible with the ECP groups of RFC 5903, RFC 5114, RFC 2409 and RFC 2412. It can also interoperate with IEEE P1363 and ANSI X9.62 for fields of characteristic greater than three, using prime curves with a cofactor of 1 and an identity key derivation function.

KT-I is mathematically and functionally equivalent to ECDSA: KT-I signatures can be verified with the ECDSA verification algorithm, and the reverse also holds.

For validation, the RFC recommends known answer tests (KATs) and consistency tests. KT-I signature creation is non-deterministic, so it is tested for consistency against verification, while verification is tested with KATs, such as those in RFC 4754. ECDH can use the test cases from RFC 5903 or RFC 5114, and the RFC gives tables mapping its notation to theirs. Integers are converted to and from octet strings with the first octet most significant.
sections.eli5: Because the recipe matches what other standards already use, programs built from it can talk to programs built from those standards. Fixed practice questions with known answers let you check your work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security level is set by the cheapest known attack. Generic attacks such as Pohlig-Hellman, Shanks' algorithm and Pollard rho work in any group, and cost roughly the square root of the group order for the last two. The RFC states that there are no known subexponential algorithms against general elliptic curve groups, though some special curves are weaker.

The basic Diffie-Hellman exchange does not protect against active attacks, so the public keys that are exchanged should be directly authenticated; authenticating only the shared secret is not sufficient. A cofactor not equal to 1 allows a number of attacks, and using a cofactor of 1 is possible and desirable.

Because the group operation does not use the parameter b, an attacker can submit a bogus point from a different curve and learn about a static private key. The defence is not to assume that every coordinate pair is a point on the curve. For signatures, curve parameters should come from a trusted source, and a collision-resistant hash such as SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 prevents existential forgery.
sections.eli5: Two things matter most: check that the other side's public number really belongs to them, and check that any point someone hands you is really on the curve. Otherwise a trickster can sneak in a fake.
